title: how one german citys struggle decarbonise is litmus test europes green  ecmii 2026 07 22
text:
July 22 - The city of Remscheid is the centre of metalworking and tooling in Germany’s industrial heartland. A glimpse of Germany’s highest railway bridge, the nearby Mungsten, offers a clue to its industrial heritage.
Germany is Europe’s largest economy, and also boasts one of its biggest concentrations of energy-intensive industries. The extent to which electrification, green hydrogen, carbon capture and storage, and thermal energy storage are adopted in Remscheid will be a litmus test for whether the entire 27-nation bloc has a chance of meeting its ambitious climate goals.
When the EU energy commissioner, Dan Jorgensen, unveiled proposals this month to double, to 46%, the share of electricity in Europe’s energy mix by 2040, it was in recognition that electrification is key ​to enabling industry to adopt new technologies and wean itself off imported natural gas.
However, when the Ethical Corporation Magazine spoke to companies in Remscheid on a recent visit, it was clear how tall an order this will be.
Roman Diederichs, joint managing director of family-owned steel forger Dirostahl, points out that the ‌400-year-old company uses around 10 times as much gas as electricity. Most of it is consumed to heat its furnaces to 1,200 degrees Celsius, then to forge the steel to make the specialist components for industries, including wind turbines.
“In (the) past, there were several changes, from water power to electricity and from coal to oil to natural gas, and now with decarbonisation discussions we are facing the question of exchanging natural gas – but for what?” he asks.
In each previous transition there had been a positive business case, but Diederichs doesn’t yet see one for electrification, especially when the industry faces severe international competition and the price of electricity in Germany is almost three times that of gas. (In the UK, by comparison, it is more than four times.)
Moreover, grid fees have “exploded” since 2021 says Diederichs, making electrification even less attractive.
German industry has already felt the impact ​of high energy prices caused by the war in Ukraine, with production in energy-intensive industries declining 15% between 2022 and 2026. No one expects it to return.
Dirostahl captures waste heat from the furnaces and uses AI to optimise some of its processes, but it has gone as far as it can with energy-efficiency measures.
Ironically, even wind ​turbine manufacturers are unwilling to pay an extra euro for lower carbon steel parts, observes Diederichs. It would be a “very positive move” if they did,
“We are not a dinosaur, but state of the art,” says Diederichs. The company is open to looking at alternative technologies, ⁠he explains, but shifting to electricity now would more than double energy costs, while adopting green hydrogen would make energy bills five times higher. On top of which there are grid fees and carbon taxes to pay.
European industry, he says, “does not want to reach decarbonisation by deindustrialisation … We have to find a way to make an alternative affordable.”
Across the city sits Steinhaus, ​Europe’s largest fresh pasta producer, making its own brand and supplying companies such as Lidl and Aldi. Again, it’s a business steeped in history, starting out over 180 years ago as a butchery.
The heat requirement at Steinhaus is a more modest 150 degrees. Burning gas generates the steam for pasteurisation, whilst electricity is used for cooling processes. Increasingly, its customers are passing on their ​Scope 3 emissions targets.
In the last 10 years, electricity consumption per metric ton of product has been cut by up to 35% in some segments. “We are constantly optimising our production processes, but it gets harder and harder to achieve additional improvements whilst staying competitive,” says head of process optimisation, Sven Hudy. The next step is direct electrification of production processes.
“Looking outside, it's actually very hot in Remscheid, and so we need to cool more, and this creates more electricity demand for our cooling and and air-conditioning processes – another important reason why we have to act. Decarbonisation is really important for us.”
Electrifying companies such as Steinhaus and Dirostahl also presents a huge challenge for local utility system operator EWR. The current electricity output for the entire city would need to expand by almost 50% to convert the Dirostahl plant alone to run on ​electricity.
Capital expenditure on the local grid is already anticipated in the hundreds of millions of euros in the coming years. Remscheid’s bus company is switching over to electric vehicles, while households are expected to install heat pumps, requiring a big programme of cable reinforcement.
Negotiations with the European Parliament and Council will determine whether the Commission’s electrification target becomes legally binding or ​remains an aspiration.
To achieve that higher electrification, the European Commission wants to see the gap between the price of gas and electricity narrowed to no more than two-fold for industry and more flexible transmission and distribution network charges.
Member-states will be asked to reduce taxes and grid charges for energy-intensive industries; to lower taxes on electricity compared to natural gas and to start to phase out fossil fuel subsidies.
The ‌Commission is also aiming ⁠to have 200 gigawatts (GW) of energy storage in place by 2030, including thermal storage, compared with 50GW today. It’s a recognition of the value storage can bring to the electricity system, to help balance the grid, says Marlene Simeon, policy director at think-tank Future Cleantech Architects (FCA).
“The commission is really trying to incentivise storage, to reward it, so industry can say ‘if I integrate these types of technologies in my process, I can get a return as well, and the payback period for all this electrification is shorter’,” says Simeon.
Because business can use storage off grid, that can help alleviate the grid bottlenecks that are dogging Europe: “I think that's where storage can play a big role in the business case for electrification,” she adds.
Notably, thermal storage technologies are now available to decarbonise sectors that require heat at less than 500 degrees Celsius, such as those used at Steinhaus.
In June, Simeon and her colleagues at the FCA took policymakers to Remscheid so they could see for themselves both the pressures facing the industrial sector and potential solutions.
Steinhaus’s Hudy anticipates the electrification plan will make investment easier. “Faster permitting, faster grid connections, faster infrastructure buildout – ​this is really good for us.”
But the barriers are not just on the policy ​side. When Steinhaus discussed the additional grid capacity needed for electrification, EWR explained it ⁠would require a new transformer station and that its implementation would take more than three years
To help industry transition, in the face of growing international competition, the Commission also wants more of the revenues from Europe’s Emissions Trading System (ETS) spent on decarbonisation.
Member-states get 80% of the 40 billion euros ($45.6 million) raised annually by the ETS, but spend less than 10% of those revenues on helping industries decarbonise. The Commission now wants them to commit 50%.
It is also proposing to slow the planned reduction of free allowances and extend their phase-out to 2038, for sectors ​covered by the carbon border adjustment mechanism (CBAM). Operating since January, the CBAM puts a price on carbon emitted during the production of imported goods in high-emitting sectors such as iron and steel.
Businesses will continue to get free allowances beyond 2030, tied to having ​a decarbonisation plan, although crucially the Commission is proposing ⁠that only 20% of the free allowances are contingent on actual investment in decarbonisation.
FCA argues the phase out timetable for allowances should remain as originally planned, so as not to punish the early first-movers.
“Of course, regulatory stability is really key for investors,” observes Simeon, so the ETS proposals could be “difficult”. However, she adds that if revenues are “really targeted, ear-marked and conditional” they could be helpful for energy intensive industries and cleantech deployment.
It’s also crucial to keep the door open for innovation, she says. So much focus has been on hydrogen or CCS, but “if I take steel, solutions could be molten-oxide electrolysis or electrowinning, maybe not now, but maybe in 10 years we could have them. So that's also how the ETS revenues should be used: on diversification, innovation and ultimately, more electrification.”
Dirostahl is ⁠unaffected by the revisions as ​it doesn’t get free allowances, but Diederichs advocates for the CBAM to be extended through supply chains, something the European Council has been considering. It wants the Commission to carry out an annual review of downstream ​products that could be included in the CBAM.
“If, further out in the future, the electricity price would really come down, so that it's affordable to run an electric furnace, then of course, we would use it, no question. But we have to bridge the near future first,” says Diederichs.
Biomethane is one such potential bridging technology, he says, as it’s less than twice the price of gas. “If the EU or German government would make more biomethane available, ​with higher priority for hard-to-abate industries, that would be very helpful – at least as a bridge technology.”
For all the threats to European industry from high energy prices, Diederichs is optimistic. “We’ve always found solutions (but) it will take some years”.
His challenge now to policymakers is to enable industry to reach the end of the bridge to a green industrial future, and sooner, rather than later.
